source.title: A Resource Model For Neural Scaling Law
source.authors: Jinyeop Song; Zi-Ming Liu; Max Tegmark; Jeff Gore

page_placements.theme: Architecture, training and regularization shape specialization

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports that its toy experiment did not show superposition, but its networks had far more neurons than tasks and it does not test the claim's overcomplete, sparse-feature setting or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites and discusses superposition, and reports its own finding of no superposition in a two-task parallel toy experiment. That setting does not test whether more sparse features than dimensions are represented by overlapping directions. Resource-allocation ratios, loss scaling, and neuron redundancy are not results measuring any listed version.
record.test_reason: The superposition result is an aside to a resource-allocation and scaling-law study. The two-task parallel network has 1000 neurons for two dense scalar inputs, so it is far from overcomplete and the inputs are not sparse. The authors note the setting differs from typical superposition conditions. No result bears on whether any version holds; the observation of monosemantic allocation under ample capacity fits V1/V2 predictions but does not test them.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a resource model (subtask loss ∝ 1/allocated neurons, plus homogeneous growth of allocation) explains scaling in their toy setups. They derive ℓ ∝ Np^-1/3, matching the Chinchilla exponent of -0.34, while allowing this may be coincidence. They list lack of superposition and neuron redundancy as side phenomena and hope the framework extends to LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses regularized toy regression networks to study neuron allocation and loss scaling; it does not reproduce the original superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that the absence of superposition occurred in a model large relative to the task complexity; the reported experiments vary task intensity and relative task weight, not overcomplete feature count.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 1000-neuron one-hidden-layer network fitting two independent x² tasks with L1/L2 penalties, each neuron served one task or was unused. There was no superposition, and the neuron ratio was about 2.35 at beta=0.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With ample width and sparsity regularization, dense independent subtasks are allocated disjoint neurons (no superposition), with allocation ratios set by relative task weight.

record.peer_reviewed: Published as a workshop paper at ICLR 2024
record.problems: The relevant superposition result is limited to a toy setting with two tasks and 1000 hidden neurons; the paper states this setting is not the typical condition for superposition. It does not test overcomplete sparse features or report a control for this result.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results measure a listed version. Resource-allocation ratios, loss-scaling results, and serial-task neuron redundancy are outside the versions' specified measures.

untested.parts: No setting with more sparse features than dimensions; no geometry or sparsity-dependent transition measured.
No capacity-limited setting; feature importance (beta) changes neuron counts but not sharing, and capacity is never binding.
No polysemantic neurons are reported, so no alternative cause is shown.
No LLM representation or SAE analysis; the Chinchilla comparison is a derived scaling exponent only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is kept. The no-superposition observation is consistent with the capacity account (no superposition without capacity pressure), but the authors themselves attribute it to the model being large relative to the task. The design (dense inputs, no overcompleteness) cannot show superposition arising, so it gives no evidence for or against V1/V2.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment has more sparse features than dimensions or measures the geometry of overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature directions or its dependence on sparsity.
The paper does not test whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
The paper does not demonstrate polysemantic neurons arising for a reason other than capacity pressure.
No LLM feature-distribution or sparse-dictionary recovery result is reported.
The paper does not measure whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: fully connected network (two tasks in parallel)
rows.stage_stated: trained toy network; training method not stated
rows.operation_detail: Checked whether neurons were shared between two parallel squared-regression tasks.

conditions.value: two independent x² regression tasks in parallel

rows.measure: Occurrence of superposition, described as one neuron representing both tasks.
rows.value: The authors report that superposition was not observed; each neuron was allocated to the first task, the second task, or was useless.
rows.note: The authors say the network size was sufficiently large relative to task complexity, unlike typical conditions for superposition. This does not test the overcomplete setting named in V1.
rows.check: Row is accurate for its own measure: no neuron was shared between the two tasks. It does not measure a version, because inputs are 2 dense features into 1000 neurons, with no capacity pressure and no sparsity of features. Baseline is correctly not stated. Its versions stay none.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, experimental setup and Results, pp. 4–6: 1000 hidden neurons; beta=0.75; alpha in [1,512]; no neuron shared between tasks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Section 3.1, experimental setup and Results, pp. 4–6: 1000 hidden neurons; beta=0.75; alpha in [1,512]; no neuron shared between tasks.

relation.reason: The authors discuss absent neuron sharing and explicitly distinguish their setting from typical superposition conditions; they neither test a listed version nor use superposition as a tool.

tranche.reason: The neuron-sharing observation tests none of V1–V6: two dense scalar inputs and 1000 hidden neurons do not instantiate V1's sparse, overcomplete setting or establish V2's capacity explanation.

source_check.notes: The allocation ratio is explicitly 2.35 ± 0.24 across eight seeds at beta=0.75. The authors' conclusion is accurately summarized: the LLM scaling derivation depends on assumptions, and its agreement with Chinchilla may be coincidental.
